speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has referred to a very difficult and delicate subject. To have retired me, for instance, four years ago would have been in singular disregard of the public interest; and to retire so many gentlemen I see opposite who are perfectly willing to serve the state in an eventuality that will never happen would be much more serious still.
The problem is one that has engaged the attention of a great many people, especially in our English speaking world, with respect to judges and commissioners and with respect to those who hold positions similar to those of judges and commissioners. We have already provided that seventy-five shall be the retiring age for county or district court judges and for

the Supreme Court of Canada; seventy is the compulsory age for retirement in many cases in the civil service, and civil servants may retire at sixty-five. But the difficulty in meeting my 'hon. friend's suggestion is this, having regard also to what vras said by my hon. friend from East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell) as to the right type of man for the chairmanship: if you say he must retire at an earlier age than seventy, he may already be occupying the position of a judge and be sixty or more. So it is a matter of extreme difficulty. I think in following the provisions of the Civil Service Act as we have, we have gone as far as we should. Although I appreciate what has been said, I should certainly not like to see this changed to sixty, because I believe it would not operate in the interests of efficiency. I think it better to leave it in the terms of the Civil Service Act, which one day must be revised, probably, having regard to the conditions. This was written into the statute on the basis that the provisions of the Civil Sendee Act would be observed.

I need hardly remind the 'hon. gentleman that one of the officials of the Canadian Pacific died while on duty, and he was nearer seventy-five than sixty-five. Recently the banks have been endeavouring to provide more positions by retiring as many of their staff as possible between sixty and sixty-five, and large numbers of them have been retired in order that the younger men might have a chance and that greater opportunities for employment might be provided. In the railways the situation is as I have indicated. In the civil service we have extended the time beyond even seventy. There are one or two members of the service that we provide for by act of parliament, in the estimates, where the age has been extended beyond seventy-five; it would be very difficult to replace these men at any age because of their accumulated experience in the particular positions they occupy, having regard to their present keen intellect and the grasp of the problems with which they

I regard this as one of the
most important clauses of the whole bill, and I think we ought to have some explanation and a discussion of it. It is something new in our legislation and covers a wide territory. For instance, it gives to the commission certain powers which no previous commission has ever had in this country. In many respects I am exceedingly glad that the body which is to administer the act will have some of the powers that are to be conferred upon it by clause 7. But there is so much ambiguity about it that it is rather difficult for me to apprehend all that is implied in the bill. One of the sections provides that the commission may do something for those who are out of work and dlo not come within the financial benefits of the bill. If this bill is to be placed on an actuarial basis and the fund is to be administered according to such an arrangement, then I find it rather difficult to see what assistance they can give, apart from financial aid, to those who are out of work for the time being or who perhaps may be permanently unemployed. I thought however that, without going further into the meaning of this section, I might ask the Prime Minister to take the house and the country into his confidence and tell us what the government have in mind at this session of parliament in relation bo those people who will not benefit by this bill when it becomes law. When the Prime Minister a few days ago moved the second reading of the bill he stated that the government had in mind some other provision to meet the unemployment situation in Canada, and I do think that now we are discussing section 7 of the bill, the Prime Minister might say, where questions of the unemployed and partially employed are covered by the bill and it is intended that those out of work shall be kept physically fit to do work when there is no work for them to do, what kind o'f work he has in mind. What does the Prime Minister intend to do for that large section of our population who at present are looking with a great deal of hope and expectation to the government to provide them in the immediate future with useful and productive work?

I was interested in the remarks of the Prime Minister a few days ago when he gave the list of those' who would be exempted from insurance under this bill. My concern at the present time is for a few hundred coal miners in my constituency, because I am at a loss to know whether or not they can be brought under this bill. They are engaged as part time employees in the coal mines for from twenty to twenty-four or twenty-eight weeks in the year, and then the rest of the time they are probably on farms or working at other occupations. I was wondering whether they could be brought under this bill, and how. These miners are having a very difficult time; they have been experiencing a difficulty in the last two years in making ends meet. I am informed that the mine owners are rather concerned about this bill because they are finding it very difficult to make ends meet, to pay their taxes, their running expenses and so on without having to meet additional costs. Under this bill will these mine owners be compelled to contribute when they employ their miners only for a certain period of the year?
I have listened with a good deal of interest to the discussion that has been going on in connection with this bill, and I have wondered whether any reason has been given so far why I should support a measure of this kind.
I represent a farming community in Saskatchewan, composed almost entirely of farmers *with the exception of the few hundred coal miners I have mentioned, and unless those miners can benefit by the act I do not know of any person in my constituency who can derive any benefit from it. If times were normal I do not believe our people would object very much to the passing of an unemployment insurance bill; but at the present time, when our farmers find it impossible to pay their taxes, I think it is hardly fair to impose additional taxation upon them. It is an axiom of our law that those who do not receive any benefit from taxes should not be taxed. I wonder what the Prime Minister has in mind for constituencies such as the one I represent. What does he intend to do by way of compensating adjustment for the money which those farmers will pay to make up their share of the dominion government's obligation? I am concerned for the moment for the part time employees in these mines, and I should like to know whether or not the owners will be compelled to pay a share of insurance.

The commission shall, a6 soon as practicable after appointment, undertake investigations-
And so forth. This is altogether a new departure in Canada. speechtext:
I did endeavour to point out that as long ago as 1919, 1920, this parliament made provisions for financial assistance to labour exchanges and that the labour exchanges have during all those years been gathering certain information which has been made available to the governments of the country. It is contemplated that the information which can be derived from investigation not by these three men themselves but from the machinery connected with the commission will enable them to have a clear appreciation of the situation with respect to the matters to which the hon. gentleman has referred. But the unemployment advisory committee is not intended to deal with matters of that kind, neither is it contemplated that it should take any part in what one might call the administrative side of the matter, but rather as citizens of repute, probably serving as a matter of public service, they will be able to give their disinterested advice upon the evidence that may be accumulated by the commission or through its instrumentality. In England this has been found to be a highly desirable committee and one that has done extraordinarily good service, but in that 92582-59
country there is a chain of responsibility that descends to the parish and the small community through the one government that, as the hon. gentleman knows, we do not have here, and one of the difficulties in a country of such vast distances as this is to have a local body that will be able to give adequate reports upon all the matters that affect employment and unemployment. In England the labour exchanges have been regarded as the basis of the success of the operation of a measure of this kind, and I believe the labour exchanges in this country will, when they are functioning as provided by this measure, render invaluable assistance along the lines that have been suggested. I trust my right hon. friend will not suggest that labour exchanges will endeavour to deprive a commission which he proposes to set up of any power or authority in that regard. But I think whoever administers government will find the labour exchanges invaluable from the standpoint of being able to collect such definite and positive information.

speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister whether the Westminster act referred to is the Unemployment Assistance Act, 1934, which was printed, according to the instructions of the House of Commons at Westminster, on December 11, 1934?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
There are two statutes to which I take it the hon. member refers. One deals with the benefits that are called unemployment assistance apart altogether from the question of unemployment insurance. The Unemployment Assistance Act of 1934 was added to the Unemployment Act of 1932 as part II thereof. It begins of course with the very local unit of administrative power and traces up to the highest point of responsibility under that statute. The poor laws, for instance, are subject to consideration in dealing with that act. There is provision for sudden ot urgent necessity in trade disputes, cases of special difficulty, suspension from the advantages of the act, and matters of that kind. That is the act to which reference was made. The Poor Relief Act, to which some reference

Unemployment Insurance

was made, went back as far as 1601, and then there is the poor law practice before 1914. All that is the historical side of the matter. And then there is the statute which is the Unemployment Assistance Act, the one to which the hon. gentleman has referred.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
I thank the right hon. gentleman. With that act of 1934, there is a lengthy memorandum explanatory of the draft made under section 32. That legislation, is very interesting, but I was greatly disappointed when I read it. I listened carefully to a broadcast given by the Prime Minister. I do not mean the Prime Minister of Canada; I mean the Right Hon. Ramsay MacDonald, and I have before me a clipping from the Montreal Star quoting that broadcast. This appeared the same day the broadcast was made, namely November 9, 1934. Mr. MacDonald spoke about this very legislation which has been referred to by some hon. gentlemen:
MacDonald Highlights.
That is the heading of the article.
Right Hon. Ramsay MacDonald, speaking at the Lord Mayor's banquet in the ancient Guildhall of London, England, at 4.10 to-day said:
"It has become quite clear that the unemployed problem of our generation calls for national planning and coordination.
To reclassify our unemployed we have made a new unemployment act, one of the greatest advances in social legislation and administration that this country has known.
We must never forget that they are human beings. A great majority of them are men and women whose distress is their misfortune."
He said that there was to be a reclassification of the unemployed. A good friend I have in Westminster was kind enough to send me the act and the memorandum, but I was very much disappointed in reading them because both of them contained nothing with regard to reclassification of the unemployed according to trade. This is vital. The other day I listened to the Prime Minister and he gave us figures from the census of 1931. We are now in 1935 and from the calendar on the table I see that this is February 18. What are the figures for February 18, 1935? Are they the figures of 1931? I remember distinctly that the census figures of the unemployed were not given in 1931 or in 1932; they were given by the Minister of Labour in 1933, two years after they were gathered. Is this reasonable? Are we posted as to the real situation of the unemployed? Paragraph (e) of the definitions reads: "continuously unemployed." There are some men who work part time and they may be considered as unemployed because their salary is not sufficient to cover the expenses of their living. There are many people who are being taken care of 
by their fathers. For instance there are farmers' sons who left for the cities, married and had children while they were working there; they have lost their jobs on account of the tariff policy of the government; they have returned home and their fathers now have to take care of them. According to this, however, they are not considered as unemployed. I defy the Prime Minister, the Minister of Labour or any other of his colleagues to give the right figures about unemployment, including those taken care of by their parents or relatives. They have no figures. They come here with the figures of the census of 1931. Bluff, humbug, deceit. Was the number of unemployed the same in 1931 as it is on February 18, 1935? Those figures are out of date. They are all right to put on the blackboard for school children, but they are not the proper figures to give to members of parliament. The Prime Minister cannot object to what I say, because once I asked him the question and he was about to reply when an hon. member who did not hear my question got up and interrupted him. Afterwards I asked him in straight language: "What are you doing to classify the unemployed? What can you do to relieve unemployment unless you have reliable figures about the numbers according to their trade?" What was his answer? His answer was: "We are doing our best in that regard." I wonder what "our best" means. I wonder if it means anything. That answer was confirmation of what I had been saying for years in this house. This request is based on logic. What does the government know about the number of unemployed according to trade? Can the Minister of Labour tell me the number of white collar unemployed in any city, town or village in this country? He does not know, neither does the Prime Minister, neither do the third rate clerks who drafted this legislation, copied it from similar legislation passed in other countries without regard to the special conditions of this country. They know nothing; they have no foundations; they build castles in the air. What for? Propaganda, that is all. I said that this afternoon and I say it again: Does the Prime Minister-for whom I have a high regard, except when he makes such statements as he sometimes does; outside the house I have great respect for him-does he say seriously to this house that he can do anything for the relief of unemployment unless he knows about their number according to trade? That is essential; it is something every one should know. I am surprised that such an eminent man refuses to inform himself about that. It has been repeated time and

Unemployment Insurance
time again that each unemployed person should be considered individually, just the same as each soldier who was wounded on the battlefield had to be looked after individually.

No, those figures are not correct; I have trans^ posed them. The number idle was 370,966, while the number losing time through illness was 87,062.
The numbers idle, per 100,000 wage earners, as shown in the final column of the 1921 census table, page A3, and in the 1931 census tables on this page, were plotted on cross-ruled paper according to the time idle in weeks, and a curve was drawn with a spline among the plotted points. From these curves were read off the probabilities of being unemployed less than one week, one to two weeks, two to three weeks, and so on. The 1921 and 1931 probabilities were not used -directly in the computation of the rates of contribution, but from these probabilities and the probabilities for the nine year period, 1922-30, the probabilities for the eleven year period, 1921-31, were computed,

Unemployment Insurance
the latter probabilities being the main basis used in determining the contributions. All of these probabilities are shown on page A8.
If it should be noted that, in drawing all of the probability curves referred to in the next preceding paragraph, the spline was sloped so as to increase the probabilities for the periods of idle time approaching zero, for it is believed that a substantial proportion of those reporting no idle time in the census year had in fact short periods of idle time. Those who had had several short periods of idle time of, say, one, two or three days, might easily forget the whole or a portion thereof in the course of the year, or might not think it worth while to report what might appear to be a trifling amount of idle time.
By drawing the curves in this manner indicated above, the average idle time as computed from the curve probabilities is larger than if the census data were adhered to more closely in drawing the curves, but there is ractically no addition to unemployed days for enefit purposes, for, under the scheme of the bill, the first nine unemployed days are excluded for benefit purposes. There is a slight reduction in the average number of weeks of contribution, and this is on the safe side.
I am perfectly willing that this section should stand, but I read this so that hon. members may have no doubt as to the basis upon which the measure has been framed. Mr. Watson, the actuary from whose report I read, is associated with the actuarial branch of our insurance department, and 'he enjoys a very high reputation. But the government believed that the members of the house would require information from some other source, and the other day I tabled a report by Mr. Wolfenden, a consulting actuary, who has given a great deal of time to this matter.
I should like to answer, if I might, one criticism, and that is that this measure should have been introduced last year. The census was completed in 1931. In the debate that arose on a resolution presented by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I promised that if we were alive before we ceased to be a government-at least before we dissolved parliament-we would ask the house to consider an unemployment insurance measure. More perhaps than hon. members opposite are concerned I have been concerned in trying to expedite this measure. It has not been easy to sift out all the figures to which I have directed attention, as shown by the census. If any hon. gentleman thinks the tabulating of the returns of a census is a simple process, all he has to do is go up to the statistical branch and observe the operation of the machines by which definite information is tabulated. That information was long in preparation and difficult of computation. Then it had
to be compared with the information obtained in 1921, and an average had to be made in order to be able to provide, with some degree of actuarial certainty, for the contingencies with which the bill deals, bringing the information down to 1934. So these figures have been framed on an eleven year period, which it is believed will be as adverse a period against the fund as it would be possible to conceive under ordinary conditions, for, as is pointed out by Mr. Watson, we would be unwise if we projected ourselves into the future with a too optimistic mind, and on the other hand we would be unfair if we dealt with the matter with a mind too pessimistic. So, taking the figures during the eleven year period ending in 1931, you have the result to which I have referred.
There is one further word I should like to say in consequence of the observation made by tire hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. In the very nature of things legislation of this kind can become operative only after it has been in force for a considerable period of time. The greatest social reformer of our modern times, dealing with this legislation, pointed out how unwise it is for a people to endeavour to predicate their position upon no change, and how desirable it il to try to look into the future for a period of at least two years. In the effort that is represented by this bill there has been an endeavour to look beyond the confines of today and visualize at least to some extent the conditions that may exist two years hence, at the lowest, so that the operation of the bill, if there were a recurrence or even a continuance of conditions of depression, would find the countiy at least equipped to meet it. The corresponding benefits, with the adjustment of benefits to the farming and labouring population, comes about through the exercise of their purchasing power on the one hand and, shall I say, so far as this is concerned, from the very earnest endeavour that has been made that even more than equally corresponding benefits should be conferred upon the agricultural population. I do not wish to interrupt, but first of all I wish to tell the right hon. gentleman opposite that I used no violent language; I was just in an indignant mood, that is all. I am pleased to note that the hon. member for Gloucester has brought up the matter to which he has just referred. The figures which the right hon. gentleman has quoted are a vindication of the policy the Liberal government followed during the nine years they were in power. Why is that so? Because the figures he has read show only a very small number of unemployed in that time. When he goes to the country he will give the figures of the working men during the time the Liberal party was in power. Let him give the figures showing the unemployed, so that the people may be in a position to subtract that number from the number who were working in 1930. Sir, the Prime Minister has been most unfair in the manner in which he has presented his figures. I have nothing to say about Mr. Watson. He may be a very honourable gentleman, and I am not attacking him. However I have quoted figures long enough to know that figures can be digested only after they
have appeared in Hansard. The Prime Minister may read tables, but who understands them? What difference does it make whether the Prime Miinster says "females, 20-5; males 30-5; both sexes 25-056"-what difference does it make? Let him give other figures. I imagine people with pencils and paper calculating these figures; they come here and say that this or that will save the country. We have had enough of that. The Prime Minister is too serious a man to give us figures of the time the Liberal party was in power, and then say to the people, "This is the number of people who will take advantage of this scheme of unemployment insurance." That is most unfair, and untrue. Why? Because there are so many unemployed now that of three men one man works, one does not work and one works only part time. The man working part time is supported by the man who works all the time. For that reason the man who works all the time has to support not only himself and his family but also the unemployed and the man who works part time. Sometimes he has many children, and the added burden is very great. To quote now figures showing conditions during the time t'he Mackenzie King government was in power is an absurd procedure.
The question asked by the hon. member for Gloucester was a timely one. Let them come here on February 18, 1935, give the actual number of unemployed and the actual number who are working, and then they will have to tell all the unemployed, " This insurance scheme is of no use to you." On the other hand the government will have to tell the people who are at work now, " We have a scheme for you. You will get something if you pay, and if your employer pays, and if this legislation is declared valid by the courts of this country. Otherwise you will get nothing." The Prime Minister has been very careful in his remarks. I have often heard him say: It is a move in the right direction. But 'he changes so often that he might change before this is put into force. He has changed about tariffs, and about many other things. He might change about this, and then the people will have nothing. But the election will be past and in the meantime his party expects to take advantage of this legislation. I mention this because it is my deep conviction that this legislation is only humbug and bluff, and we are not here to listen to humbug and bluff.
We hear hon. gentlemen opposite speak of the legacy received from the former administration. I see one of my friends on the
Unemployment Insurance

treasury benches smile at that. He knows he has used that language. I also see another friend of mine from the province of Quebec speaking to one of his colleagues when he should be listening to this. I have heard him say over the radio: What a legacy we received from the Libeial party! Well, the legacy he received was the figures which the right hon. gentleman has just quoted about the numbers of men who were working. Let him look at the change in 1930 as compared with 1929, the small drop in the number of men who were working in 1930 at the time when the Tories were paying people to wear white buttons and parade as unemployed in order to disturb the meetings of my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition. That is what was done, and it was just bluff and humbug in 1930 as it is bluff and humbug now.
During the adjournment I happened to meet Rip Van Winkle, who had been asleep since July, 1930, when he heard the present Prime Minister say at Moncton, " I will end unemployment or perish in the attempt." He asked me: "What is going on now in the house"? I told him: "Unemployment insurance," and he asked me: "How is that? Unemployment should have been cured before now. Who is putting it through"? I said that it was the hon. member for West Calgary, and Rip Van Winkle asked: "Who is the hon. member for West Calgary? Surely he has been defeated, because if he had become prime minister there would have been no unemployment in this country." I replied: "No, Rip. It is a most extraordinary thing. He did not perish in the attempt, but the country has perished in the attempt, and the number of unemployed is now so great that he is afraid to state the correct number of unemployed to the House of Commons."
The Prime Minister says he will come to their rescue, but how can he when he does not know their number, does not know where they are or how they are? The only thing he knows is the amount that was paid by this government to the provincial governments, and about some schemes to give a chance to profiteers to make money out of building wharves and things like that. That is all he knows about. Let me tell him, as I have very often told his supporters, and the members of the government, that they should create a wall around him to give him time to think about the business of this country, instead of being importuned by callers who come seeking jobs. I know very well that if the right hon. gentleman had been left alone, instead of being encouraged
* Mr. Pouliot.]
in this policy of desperation, in this nefarious policy, by people who call themselves his friends but are not, the policy of this government would have been entirely different. But to-night I have the satisfaction of my life. I see the vindication of the Liberal party, a vindication of the Liberal policy during the ten years the Liberal party was in power, and in future when one hears any Tory member opposite say "Look at the legacy we received from the Liberal party," the reply will be, "Remember Mr. Watson's figures which were read and taken as his own by the Prime Minister on the night of February 18,
1935." Then they will be just as dumb as ministers of the crown.

117,000	were unemployed at that time. That is, the number had been increased by 200,000 in that one year. I quote the figures as given to the house by the Prime Minister on September 10, 1930, at page 63 of Hansard:
I find that at present in the province of Alberta there are 5,155 unemployed; during the winter it is contemplated that that number will reach 6,650. In British Columbia at the present time the unemployed number 7,692 and it is expected that during the winter that number will increase to 14,700. In the province of Saskatchewan the present number given is 5.276 and it is expected to rise during the winter to 8,201. In Manitoba the figure is now 6.950, with a possible 9,600 in the winter. In Ontario the figure is given as 49,367, rising to 82,214.
I might interject here that in the city of Toronto alone there are at present some 26,000 families on relief. The Prime Minister went on:
In Quebec the present number is 41,190, as against an anticipated number of 49,290. In New Brunswick the present number is 500 and
it is expected it may reach 2,850. In Nova Scotia the present number is 1,800 and it may rise to 2,350.
Prince Edward Island is the only province not mentioned in the list. Later on the Prime Minister says:
It will be observed that the present number is something over 117,000, and it is believed that number will approximate 177,000 during the winter.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
I hope not. I am glad to hear the Prime Minister say that. Under the British act there is a provision which compels employers to notify the minister-in this case it would be the commission, I presume-in the case of the discharge of any young worker between the ages of fourteen and eighteen. The object of that, so far as the act seems to be concerned, is that they may be instructed to attend compulsorily some local training camp, or industrial centre, as it is euphoniously termed. If children of fourteen or fifteen years of age fail to attend, action may be taken against the parents and the parents may be fined a
Unemployment Insurance

certain sum for not compelling their child or children to attend such an industrial centre. Furthermore, the minister can then take proceedings under the Education Act of 1921 or the Education, Scotland, Act, of 1918, or the Day and Industrial Schools Act, Scotland, of 1893, to remove the young workers entirely from the parents' control and order them to be placed in the charge of other relatives or a person named by the minister, or order their attendance in a reformatory school. In other words, the minister may order young workers to enter such a place for a period that may be three years or less, at least until they are eighteen years of age. The reason for that in Great Britain is clear. It is that the benefits under their act appear to be quite insufficient to enable the parents adequately to take care of themselves and their children. I am content that the Prime Minister is seized of the great social importance of having the children kept in the home, especially at that extremely delicate age, fourteen to sixteen, the age of adolescence, a most dangerous period for both male and female. I would suggest therefore that in the consideration of any scheme under this clause of the bill regard is had to the necessity for taking proper precautions to see that the children are not taken from the parents unless there is some other reason, for instance, criminal taint or mental taint or something of that sort. If the parents are satisfactory citizens; if they are doing the best they can, they should be assisted financially in sending their children to suitable schools in the vicinity, and even in going to high school, but the children should never be taken from under the care of the parents. I sincerely trust the Prime Minister, although he has no children, will see that the minister, if he happens to be in control, will take that fact into due consideration. I am frankly opposed to the British system in this regard.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
I think the point is very well taken, but I think also the hon. member for Bow River will at once admit that conditions that obtain in Great Britain are not similar to those that obtain in this country. For instance, our truancy acts and compulsory attendance in schools are entirely different from what they were in England at one time; I think there has been some modification during the last two years, although I am not quite certain as to that. In Ontario I think children are compelled under compulsory provisions of the statute and of the Truancy Act to attend school until they are sixteen; that is my recollection. In Alberta

we have somewhat the same provisions. In Great Britain they endeavoured to raise the age to sixteen and there was a great deal of difficulty about the matter. I do not think the hon. gentleman need fear any effort to enforce the provisions of the statute along the lines he has suggested, at least not while this government is in power.

speechtext:
Some discussion took place before recess that should have taken place on this section, as to the question of appointments by the civil service commission. I suggest to the Prime Minister that subsection 2 of section 8 is ambiguous. It reads:
For the purposes of any investigation, or for any other purpose of this act, the commission may, subject to the approved of the governor in council, from time to time temporarily employ such persons of technical and professional attainments as the commission may deem necessary.
Unemployment Insurance

Taken, in conjunction with subsection 1 it indicates to me that all technical and professional appointments will be made under patronage, because subsection 1 simply says that the commission may employ, pursuant to the Civil Service Act, "officers, clerks, and employees;" it does not mention technical or professional services of any kind. If the Prime Minister would change the wording of subsection 1 very slightly, as as to make it read:
The commission may employ such officers, clerks, employees and such persons of technical and professional attainments for the purposes of this act as the commission may deem necessary-
-then the situation would be much clearer. As it stands now it would appear that technical and professional appointments can be made only under subsection 2.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: The bill as written exactly represents the intention of the government. It refers first to the permanent employees of the commission; they are to be appointed by the civil service commission. Temporary employees, experts for any particular purpose, are appointed by the governor in council; it has been so with respect to such matters in all countries, and I suppose will continue to be. Where you do not desire to employ an expert continuously, or where you engage, as we have, the services of a professor from one of the universities, or a consulting actuary, he is treated as being an expert for a specific purpose. It will be observed that the word "temporarily" governs the whole provision-"temporarily employ such persons of technical and professional attainments as the commission may deem necessary." When the commission deems them necessary for temporary employment the governor in council must approve.

speechtext: Has the Prime Minister any idea how many officers and employees will be required for administration?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
This starts with the labour exchange as the lowest unit, and the communities will be divided into sections having regard to the size of the country. Perhaps the maritime provinces, the two large central provinces and the west will comprise the separate units, or there may be four, five or six. The number of employees will vary, of course. At first it may require a little larger number than later, because it will be necessary to get in some collected form the information which is available from the local communities. The exchange offices already have the basis of that information, as the right hon. gentleman knows, and the extent to which it will have to be amplified will depend upon the detail with which the commission will require the information to be furnished. I have formed no estimate as to the number, because, as is known, from year to year we vote a sum of money to maintain these labour offices. That sum of money would now be made available for the maintenance of these labour exchange offices, and in large centres of industrial activity such as the two central provinces there would be a vastly greater number of employees than in the smaller industrial centres, represented for instance by the maritime provinces or by the agricultural communities of Saskatchewan or Alberta, in part, although Alberta would have a considerable number by reason of its industrial activities as a result of its mineralization and lumbering. I have not formed any estimate as to the number, but I will make

Unemployment Insurance
further inquiries and ascertain if it is possible to form an idea as to the number that will be required.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: That is a very important factor, because if this act is to be a federal measure it must be apparent at once that the machinery the provinces have for this purpose can be of no service whatever. In the provinces, where they have the administration of factory, mine and shop acts, they have at hand practically all that is required in the way of staff to administer many of these social measures, but if the federal government is taking it as a federal obligation it will involve, to a considerable extent, I should imagine, the creation of what is sometimes spoken of as a bureaucracy, considering that it will be all new work for the federal government to undertake; and I have no doubt it will require a considerable number of officers throughout the different provinces. Could the Prime Minister indicate in regard to the officers and employees, not the stenographers and such, but the main employees, whether the number would run to five thousand or ten thousand?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
I think the right hon.
gentleman has imagined a larger number than I have even thought of. The employment offices, for which in times past we have really supplied the money, under the reorganization will carry on a good deal of this work, and the Department of Labour, which now carries on investigations all over Canada through fair wage officers and so on, together with the inspection of the employment offices, will be able to continue that function. It is through these officers rather than through the administrative machinery of the provinces, at least in western Canada, that this work is carried on. The reports made under the factory and coal mines acts will in no sense be interfered with by this legislation; neither will there be any duplication of effort in that regard. The employment offices have been the medium through which employers have sought employees and employees have sought employment, since they were established in 1919. Now it is proposed to increase their efficiency, but not in any sense to duplicate the effort of the provinces in dealing with their social problems, just as they have relied on these exchanges since 1920 in connection with their employment difficulties. I will make inquiries, however.

I suggest that if we confine ourselves to the numbers as they appear in the printed bill we will avoid confusion; the numbers can be changed afterwards. Section 10 of the bill deals with the matter of the commission organizing an 
employment service for the dominion. The Prime Minister has already stated we have an employment service which is to be taken over. Is the clause sufficiently broad?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: As I explained to the committee, we have these offices. The extent to which they may discharge the duties called for by this bill is an altogether different question. To the extent to which it may be possible to utilize them, it is proposed so to do, but this measure gives the commission a free hand in the organization of the employment service of the country. To restrict them in the first instance might fasten upon them inefficient persons, and one of the weaknesses I have experienced in my short official life has been that there is no statutory provision for getting rid of the inefficient person; once a civil servant he is a civil servant forever. This provision would enable the commission to organize their service on a basis which they think will be efficient.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I refer to this not in any critical sense but rather to avoid difficulties later. If we have an employment service, as it is at present organized under a department which has a responsible minister and deputy minister, a department for which this parliament makes appropriations in the estimates, and we have also a commission which is given its power under a separate act and receives its own appropriations, we could hardly have those two authorities working side by side without conflict.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
I think the right hon.
gentleman will follow me when I say that people charged with a responsibility such as that with which the commission will be charged would not desire to be compelled to accept A, B and C. But it has been found in practice-at least it has been my experience- that any effort to transfer services from one direction to another does not meet with the success one would desire. The real reason is a weakness in our civil service law. I have explained on more than one occasion that the weakness is this: No matter how inefficient an individual may be, there is no provision for terminating his service, as the private employer does, except for age or for continued inability to discharge his duties. And in I would not say many, but in several cases at least that have come under my observation, had it been a private enterprise undoubtedly the employer would have indicated to the employee, because of his failure to discharge his duties, the desirability of his seeking employment elsewhere. One of the great benefits

Unemployment Insurance
of civil service employment of which one is constantly reminded lies in that fact. I gave my opinion publicly on the point; I do not think it was accepted with very good grace, but I at least mentioned it, and it has been my observation that it was an absolutely sound statement to make, namely that once you get into the service and become a permanent employee, then the statutory increases must follow as a matter of course. Of course that is not the law at all. The law of this country is that statutory increases are based upon merit, upon meritorious service. Un^ fortunately the feeling has grown up that the statutory increase is a matter of right and of course, but under the provisions of the law, as I read them, that is not so. One of the difficulties in practice, and I believe the right hon. gentleman will agree, would 'be the transferring of services, and the possibility-and I use the word "possibility"-of making it more or less difficult for the new board sucessfully to function.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I have had the impression that the immediate and ultimate aim behind the measure was to form a commission which would gradually take over all these social services, so far as the federal government is concerned, and that this body would have to do with unemployment insurance, unemployment exchanges, old age pensions and, probably, health insurance, which may be added in the course of time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: That is dealt with here, yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
And that all
these social services would come under the commission, which would deal with these matters in a large way. If that is so I should think that as these services are now being performed in part by the Department of Labour there would be some provision under which the Department of Labour would be relieved of them. Surely it cannot be intended to have two bodies carrying on unemployment exchanges and two bodies administering old age pensions; there should be one body which would take the whole matter in hand, either through a commission outside the government service altogether or through a department of labour with enlarged functions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
I believe the right hon. gentleman's opinion and the opinion I hold are very much alike. There is nothing in the measure which discloses, as he has properly said, the manifest intention of legislation of this type, to endeavour to ensure the 92582-60
efficient administration of social services under a commission which would be set up for the purpose. He has fairly stated what is in the back of my mind; whether I live to see it carried into effect is another matter. But to transfer them by a section of the measure from one body to another is not in my judgment at the moment a proper way to do it. The right hon. gentleman will recall that the provincial authorities have at present a relation to the employment exchanges-labour exchanges-and it is the intention to cooperate with them for the purpose of seeing how this section, and the provisions of this measure may be brought into harmony with their own interests, as they are at present carried on under existing legislation. We supply some of the people and they supply some of them; we supply part of the money. It will be recalled it is a sort of joint enterprise. As soon as the commission is appointed it is proposed that they shall discuss the whole situation with the provinces, and, to the extent that it may be possible,, bring their operations in harmony with what the provinces have heretofore done in connection with labour exchanges, under the legislation which is already upon the statute books. If it becomes desirable to make the necessary amendments they will be made in the act relating to labour-I forget the name of the statute at the moment-and in the Old Age Pensions Act. The right hon. gentleman has correctly read what was in my mind, but it is not in any sense indicated in the sweep of this measure at the moment. It depends, of course, upon the human element in making effective the provisions of a statute so as to secure if possible some system of uniformity in the administration of these social services. As I said to the right hon. gentleman this afternoon, we have had considerable difficulty in connection with old age pensions, and I doubt not that he already saw the beginnings of that. We have had to make investigations at times that were most unpleasant because of the effort made to retain a position of effective independence and at the same time to receive the benefits of the Old Age Pensions Act. That has gone on on quite a large scale in more than one part of the dominion. It is unnecessary to make any public statement with reference to it, but that has been the fact. I have in my mind just what the right hon. gentleman has said, but the realization of it is altogether a different thing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
The intention then is to leave all existing services as they are, enacting this as a separate measure and

Unemployment Insurance

ultimately working towards a possible transfer of the one to the other. Inasmuch as there is some question, to put it mildly, as to the validity of the act, I think that is probably the course that should be taken. It is unfortunate that before putting through legislation to effect that end we have to wait to see whether or not the act is valid; otherwise what will now require two or three different enactments might have been accomplished in one.

Mr. iNBILL: I have an amendment to move to this section. I want to put it on Hansard so that it may be considered over night. I would move as subsection 5:
There shall not be maintained at any employment office what is known as a "blacklist."
There is a great deal of what is called labour unrest in Canada to-day. I do not know that it is anywhere more manifest than it is in British Columbia. The unrest in the labour element is being played on by certain parties, not altogether for the public good; it is being capitalized. So far as British Columbia is concerned, I do not know whether there is a more fruitful source of that discontent than the existence of what is known as the blacklist. Its existence is vehemently denied by some employers, frankly admitted by others, and of course firmly believed in by the labour element, who claim that they have absolute proof of it. In British Columbia, quite a number of years ago, we did away with private employment offices and centralized all work of that kind in government offices. Possibly it was the only way it could
Unemployment Insurance

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
be done, by simply prohibiting anyone, endeavouring to procure work for anyone else, to .be paid for it. But it did not prohibit people from doing so for nothing. Perhaps they had in mind patriotic associations, or such as the Young Men's Christian Association, which might try in a voluntary way to get work for people. The employers got round the law by either individually or through associations in the particular industry, employing a man to run an employment office, and it is in the operation of these offices that the blacklist exists. They are not employment offices in the sense of the act, though they are that to all intents and purposes, because they are run by a particular company or association of companies. A man sees a position marked up on the blackboard. He knows he can fill it and he applies, stating his qualifications. He proves to be absolutely competent and experienced at the job, and the employment agent is inclined to take him on. He asks his name and then goes behind a screen or turns to a list and comes back and says, "We don't want you." The man asks why not. The agent insists that he is not wanted and takes the man standing behind this applicant, a man less qualified and less experienced. The first applicant is turned down because he is on the blacklist.
I met a number of workers a few months ago; as a matter of fact they were strikers. Some people called them red, but if they were red they were reasonably red. The conditions were such that they might have expressed themselves in violent and vehement language, but they did not; they were reasonable. Putting things together I decided that a great deal of the trouble lay in the existence of the blacklist. I told the men that I had been an employer myself and fully realized that it was impossible to say to an employer that someone else could dictate to him whom to fire and hire. I pointed out that a business could hardly be run on that basis, that the man who employed labour and furnished the money should have the right to say whether he would employ a certain man or not; and certainly he had a right to fire him. But that should not go on forever and especially should not apply to other employers in the same industry. That is where the blacklist comes in. A man may have some words with his immediate boss, a small straw boss, in the dull and cold gray light of the morning when he is rather stiff in the joints. They are both grouchy; their boots are tight; they had been working in the wet the day before.

they have a few words and one says some-rhing to the other. They are both perfectly good men, but either the boss fires the worker or the worker beats him to it and says he will quit anyhow. A card is then filled out by the foreman when the man leaves, and this card gives his pedigree. One of the questions asked on the card is: "Would you employ this man again?" If he says no, that man's chance of a job in that industry not with that employer merely but in that industry in British Columbia-is damned for all time. That is the curse of the situation.
I told these men that if the boss fired a man for cause and they proposed to force him to take the man back, they would also perhaps run up against the situation that if the employment office sent them to a place they did not want to go, they would have to go. They said they were prepared to put up with that because they had to do it now; if they refused to go, they are placed on the blacklist.
I do not propose that it should be done by drastic action; I do not think that an employer should be forced to employ someone he does not want, and vice versa. It could be done by reasonable regulation. It might be arranged that if a man were fired from a certain company he should not be sent back to the same employer within say a year, and that would give time for feelings to die down. In the meantime there would have been a change of men and afterwards there would be no friction if he went back after the lapse of a year. In the same way, if a man quit an employer, whatever the reason might be, he should not be compelled to go back to the same employer within a specified time, which should also be reasonable. Apart from that, they should be sent out in the order in which they applied and if they were qualified for the position they would have to go and be taken. In that way men would not be thrown out of a livelihood as they can be at the present time by reason of the blacklist, simply because two grouchy men get together and curse each other. I said to these men that if they would accept a thing like that it might be abused and we might find a man saying to his boss, "You can't fire me because I can appeal to the law and you will have to take me back." The answer was that it is done in other industries. They named the railway companies in which boards of appeal, composed of some of the higher officers and some of the men, pass upon these matters. There is a report

Unemployment Insurance
every month reciting instances in which railway servants in the lower ranks have appealed on account of dissatisfaction with regard to services or wages, often in connection with their runs, and the case is decided by the board of appeal. There is no friction and the result is that for many years there has not been a railway strike. They made the further point that they themselves would work to prevent any abuse of it because it would be to their advantage to have such a system in force.
I suggest that this might be allowed to stand. It is something new I have sprung on the committee, and it might be made to apply only to British Columbia. Certainly, however, it would be an excellent thing. Some hon. member suggests that the employment agencies be done away with. I would say certainly. We have done away with them in British Columbia except in the instances I have named. It would be a good thing if it was only giving a lead in the dominion offices if they inaugurated some system whereby there would be no suggestion of this blacklist by which men, for a mere whim of somebody else, may be deprived, not of their job-that is a trivial matter; they could get another one-but of any employment at all, because the blacklist goes right down the line in the industry concerned. There is no question about that; if anyone wants instances, I can give them.
In another case, a big employer of labour -he is not in my district and I can tell the story-told me that the system they arranged was to send out a spy periodically. He did not call the man a spy; he called him an investigator. This investigator got a job; he was sent up ostensibly as one of the employees. He snooped around; of course he had to justify himself and do something for his money. The scheme worked like this: he would sidle up to a man and say: "'pretty lousy job" or "pretty lousy grub here." If the man said yes, he was reported as having said that the grub was lousy and he was dissatisfied. He would be let out within a week or two; he would not know why. He would be told: "Here is your money," and he would not get any work again in that place. That is the way blacklists get started. I would be glad if the Prime Minister could see his way clear to allowing this clause to stand so that he, his colleague the Minister of Labour and officials of that department could consider this question.

Mr. MaoINNIS:	The hon. member for
Comox-Alberni has raised a question that is of great importance to many people. I do not however agree that the basis of the blacklist is as simple as the hon. member believes it to be; at least that is not my understanding. I think the blacklist arises from the very fundamental fact that generally employers in this country are opposed to the organization of their employees in industrial organizations or in trade unions. In certain trades such as railroading, street railway 'occupations and certain stabilized trades of that kind, employees have become organized; their organizations have become well established and they have agreements with their employers. Where an agreement of that kind exists, it is almost impossible to institute a blacklist. But if we take less sheltered industries, particularly lumbering and to some extent mining, employers in those industries have opposed with every means at their disposal their employees forming any kind of organization.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Is the hon. member referring to British Columbia?
Mr. MaoINNIS:	Not only in British
Columbia, but throughout Ontario, Quebec and every other part of Canada. Employers are in the business for making profits and trades organizations militate to some extent against the making of profits, although in some cases where the employees have been organized for some time, employers believe it is good policy to have them organized because they consider men who are intelligent enough to organize will give better service than those who are not. But you cannot get that into the heads of the lumber barons, at least not in British Columbia, and I doubt if you can in Quebec. In the lumber industry on the Pacific coast the blacklist extends not only over British Columbia, but also into the northwest Pacific states, Washington and Oregon. As a matter of fact the employers themselves are very strongly organized but they object strenuously
Unemployment Insurance

to their employees organizing. I have worked for employers and I have been called up before the superintendent and told, "Our investigators have made a certain report upon you. We are sorry we have to have these investigators but the management deems them essential." These men act not only as investigators but as agents provocateurs. They get the men to start organizing and when they have done so, they will report to the employer that certain men are ringleaders. These men are then called on the carpet and sent out of the camp. From then on they are debarred from getting any employment in this particular industry. I do not know whether the proposal made by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi, which I am satisfied was made in all sincerity, will meet the situation. But if it does not, then this government should take positive and definite steps to encourage organization among the workers in industry, because there is no other way in which legislation passed by governments can be enforced than by strong organizations of the employees concerned.

I am sorry I cannot
accept the amendment. In the first place it would serve no useful purpose. No government department operating under a commission would maintain a blacklist. Lastly, if there were any difficulty about the matter it could be dealt with by regulations, for which the bill provides in section 38, and which can be as far-reaching as may be necessary. I do not think, however, that one should contemplate the possibility of an organization of this kind maintaining a blacklist. Its job, its obligation, will be just the opposite. I think on reflection the hon. member will conclude that it is undesirable to press his amendment. On the other hand if he desires that the committee should look further into it, there is no reason why the section should not stand in order that the amendment which he proposes as subsection 5 should be considered.

speechtext:
I appreciate the Prime
Minister's action. Of course I did not suggest that the government office would run a blacklist; it would be the employer who would enforce it, as he said. It would be desirable to do away with all private employment agencies, as we have done partially in British Columbia; then when the government office proposes to send a man to a certain employer and he says "I will not take him because he is on my blacklist," it would be for the government to say; "You will have to." Lest

there should be any suggestion that this is going to operate unfairly against the employer, may I say I am satisfied that a large number of employers would welcome it. I think in view of the amendment suggested by the hon. member (Mr. Neill) this committee should be informed of what is probably one of the reasons for his suggesting it. I am inclined to agree with my colleague from Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis) when he suggests that more encouragement should be given to employees in industry to organize themselves so that they can negotiate better with their employers. But it is accepted as a fact by many people in Canada to-day that during the past twelve or thirteen months men were sent into our lumber industry from one end of Canada to the other for the one and sole purpose of disorganizing the industry. There are many, and I am one, who think that these .people were sent into this country by agents of Russia who were disturbed at the quantity of lumber that this country was sending out in competition with them. We had men sent into the industry in British Columbia and other parts of Canada who were agitating and who could not 'be satisfied no matter what was given them. They were not there endeavouring to improve conditions; they were there to disturb the industry. I think that is one of the reasons for the suggested amendment. True, I do not think there is any question that there are men on the blacklist in British Columbia to-day as far as the lumber industry is concerned, and I think many of these men will be kept there until they show that they are not going to be affected by these professional, paid agitators who come there to destroy our industry. And while I am quite prepared to support any organization of employees for the purpose of enabling them to negotiate with the employers, I am not going to put a weapon in the hands of agitators so that an employer can be forced to employ them in order that they may disorganize our business.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I do not wish to prolong this discussion, but I wish to make it clear that this blacklist is not something which has been in existence only during the past year; it has existed on the Pacific coast since 1919. During the war when labour was scarce and the lumber industry very active the lumber workers built up a strong organization, but when labour became more plentiful and the employers wanted to take advantage of the state of the labour market, everything possible was done to smash the labour organizations. And ever since that time the blacklist has been in existence. While I am quite satisfied that there are a few individuals who are not interested in organizing for legitimate purposes but are possibly more interested in disorganizing, I am quite convinced from my own experience of twenty-five years in the labour movement that satisfied employees cannot be led to follow agitators of that kind.

But the point I desire to make is that while agreeing wholly that harmonious relations between employer and employed are the basis of success in any industry, I cannot think that the insertion of a subsection such as this in a statute dealing with a commission that has such wide responsibility is justifiable. Obviously you cannot force an employer to take a given employee. That is the real point to which I direct attention. And as you cannot compel him to do it without violating all the rules that have heretofore governed the relations between employer and employee, I suggest that to place such a provision in the statute would do violence to our general appreciation of the understanding that should

speechtext: There are certain exceptions under which the employee is not compelled to accept employment.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Quite so; that is provided in the statute itself.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: The clause stands?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
I promised to let it stand if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Neill) so desires.
Section stands.
On section 12-Collection of information.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: In the fourth line of subsection 2 "failure to comply with any such request" is made an offence against the act, but there is no time stated within which such failure to comply may occur. I would direct that to the attention of the Prime Minister. I think some time limit should be stated.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: One of the difficulties in stating a time in any statute of this kind is that you must have regard to distances and geography. The law implies a reasonable time; that is why no such words are included. If, for instance, I asked the hon. gentleman to supply information and said if he did not supply it within twenty-four hours proceedings would be taken against him; if he was in Vancouver and I was in Winnipeg or Ottawa, that would not be treated as of any importance at all. The real implication of the law is a reasonable time, and I think the hon. member will agree that to state any length of time would be destructive of the very purpose he has in mind.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Subsection 2 of section 12 reads:

The commission may request any person to make written returns of such information as the commission may deem necessary for the purposes of this act, and failure to comply with any such request shall be an offence-
Of course this is a commission the personnel of which we do not know at the present time, nor do we know the tribunal that will try this suggested offence, but I do think that this subsection is too broad as it stands. The commission may request information which the party is unable to furnish.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Then he could not be
fined.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Yes, he could under this subsection. I submit that the words "without reasonable cause" should be included.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: That is implied.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I do not think so, under this wording.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I think if the hon. member will observe the language of the section he will modify his view. Subsection 1 contemplates the collection of information concerning employers requiring workers and workers seeking employment, the same to be made available to the employment offices. Then they may request returns for the purposes of this act, and failure to comply with that request is constituted an offence. If reasonable time is not given there can be no conviction; if the information sought is not information under the act there can be no conviction. So, as the law implies a reasonable time, and having due regard to the conditions that govern the whole provision, namely the purposes of the act, I submit that the section i3 properly drafted.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
May I point out that the section reads:
-such information as the commission may deem necessary for the purposes of this act-[DOT]
I think we might include the words "within the knowledge of such person."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: That is implied.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I submit not, as the section is drafted.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Why not
add "within a reasonable time" since there is no time specified?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Vancouver-Burrard directed attention to that point. The law implies a reasonable time. To fix a given period would be impossible, having regard to distances. I think it is quite clear, under the decisions of the courts, that

Radio in Southern Alberta
the law implies that a reasonable time must be given. What is a reasonable time depends, as one judge has said, upon the circumstances of each case. If it was not difficult to obtain the information it might not be unreasonable to expect it the next day.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
I suggest that it would
be necessary to send a registered notice under that section, which would indicate that the time must be reasonable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
It is perfectly obvious
that there could be no conviction unless it was proved that the notice had been received.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 13-Local committees.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I notice that no provision has been made for the remuneration and expenses of these local committees.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: That is true, and the hope is that these local committees may be glad to give some service to their communities with respect to these matters. But there is provision later on, in a broad and general way, by which some honorarium may be paid. It is not intended that they shall be paid officials in that sense at all.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 14 (as printed; now section 13) -Advances to workers seeking employment.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
This section deals with the
question of transferring men who are out of work to sections of the country where employment may be found for them. It involves a rather complicated question that may require a good deal of discussion, and I would ask the Prime Minister to call it eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I can see no good purpose in having this section stand, since it is a simple clause, but if the hon. gentleman desires to have that done I shall accede to his request.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
It is eleven o'clock now, in
any case.
Section stands.
Progress reported.
